items.stem: Which is a chemical change?
items.answer: magnesium burning in air
items.markingKey: A new substance (magnesium oxide) forms.

items.stem: Which is a physical change?
items.answer: water freezing
items.markingKey: No new substance; only the state changes.

items.stem: Explain why dissolving salt in water is a physical change.
items.answer: No new substance is formed; the salt can be recovered unchanged by evaporating the water.

items.stem: Classify each change as physical or chemical: water being electrolysed; silver tarnishing; steam condensing on a window; sugar dissolving in water.
items.answer: water being electrolysed: chemical; silver tarnishing: chemical; steam condensing on a window: physical; sugar dissolving in water: physical
items.markingKey: water being electrolysed: chemical; silver tarnishing: chemical; steam condensing on a window: physical; sugar dissolving in water: physical. 1 mark per two correct [2]

items.stem: Yusuf heats 6.18 g of white zinc carbonate, ZnCO₃, in a test tube. The solid turns yellow when hot, white when cool and a gas is given off that turns limewater milky. A separate sample of wax is heated: it melts and then solidifies again on cooling. (a) Write the symbol equation for the decomposition. (b) Explain why the mass of the test tube and contents decreases.
items.answer: (a) ZnCO₃(s) → ZnO(s) + CO₂(g) (b) carbon dioxide gas escapes

items.stem: Which statement describes a physical change?
options: A precipitate forms from two solutions.
A gas is produced by a reaction.
No new substance is formed and the change is easily reversed.
items.answer: No new substance is formed and the change is easily reversed.
items.markingKey: Physical: same substance, easily reversible.

items.stem: Explain why heating hydrated copper(II) sulfate is a chemical change even though it can be reversed by adding water.
items.answer: A new substance (anhydrous copper(II) sulfate, white) and water are formed; chemical bonds to the water of crystallisation are broken, and there is an energy change.

items.stem: A student says that boiling water is a chemical change because a gas is formed. Explain why this is incorrect.
items.answer: The gas is steam, which is still water (H₂O); only the state changes, so it is a physical change.

items.stem: Classify each change as physical or chemical: iron rusting; a match burning; copper(II) sulfate crystals being ground into a powder; water being electrolysed; steam condensing on a window; ice melting.
items.answer: iron rusting: chemical; a match burning: chemical; copper(II) sulfate crystals being ground into a powder: physical; water being electrolysed: chemical; steam condensing on a window: physical; ice melting: physical
items.markingKey: iron rusting: chemical; a match burning: chemical; copper(II) sulfate crystals being ground into a powder: physical; water being electrolysed: chemical; steam condensing on a window: physical; ice melting: physical. 1 mark per two correct [3]

items.stem: Zara heats 2.47 g of green copper(II) carbonate, CuCO₃, in a test tube. The solid turns black and a gas is given off that turns limewater milky. A separate sample of wax is heated: it melts and then solidifies again on cooling. (a) Give two pieces of evidence that heating copper(II) carbonate is a chemical change. (b) Write the symbol equation for the decomposition.
items.answer: (a) colour change; gas produced (CO₂); not reversed on cooling (b) CuCO₃(s) → CuO(s) + CO₂(g)
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) [2]

items.stem: Which change increases the rate of reaction between marble chips and hydrochloric acid?
options: using powdered marble instead of chips
items.answer: using powdered marble instead of chips
items.markingKey: Larger surface area → faster reaction.

items.stem: Explain why food is stored in a refrigerator.
items.answer: Lower temperature slows the reactions (including those of microorganisms) that cause food to decay.

items.stem: Explain why a catalyst is useful in industry even though it is not used up.
items.answer: It speeds up the reaction so that products are made faster and at lower temperature, saving energy and cost; it can be reused.

items.stem: Amara varies the conditions for the reaction of iron with hydrochloric acid, keeping the mass of solid and volume of acid the same. experiment 1: filings, 1.00 mol/dm³ acid, 20 °C; experiment 2: powder, 1.00 mol/dm³ acid, 30 °C; experiment 3: filings, 1.00 mol/dm³ acid, 30 °C. Which experiment has the fastest initial rate?
items.answer: experiment 2
items.markingKey: Experiment 2 has conditions at least as favourable in every factor (concentration, temperature, surface area) and better in at least one.

items.stem: Samuel, a student in Kathmandu, reacts calcium carbonate with nitric acid, using the same mass of solid and volume of acid each time. experiment 1: large lumps, 0.250 mol/dm³ acid, 25 °C; experiment 2: small chips, 2.00 mol/dm³ acid, 35 °C; experiment 3: large lumps, 2.00 mol/dm³ acid, 35 °C; experiment 4: large lumps, 0.250 mol/dm³ acid, 35 °C. Put the experiments in order of initial rate, fastest first, and explain your order.
items.answer: Order: 2 > 3 > 4 > 1. Higher concentration, higher temperature and smaller pieces (larger surface area) each increase the rate.
items.markingKey: order 2 > 3 > 4 > 1 [2]; explanation referring to each factor varied [2]

items.stem: Felix, a student in Jakarta, reacts zinc with sulfuric acid, using the same mass of solid and volume of acid each time. experiment 1: small granules, 2.00 mol/dm³ acid, 20 °C; experiment 2: small granules, 0.250 mol/dm³ acid, 20 °C; experiment 3: powder, 2.00 mol/dm³ acid, 40 °C; experiment 4: small granules, 2.00 mol/dm³ acid, 40 °C. Put the experiments in order of initial rate, fastest first, and explain your order.
items.answer: Order: 3 > 4 > 1 > 2. Higher concentration, higher temperature and smaller pieces (larger surface area) each increase the rate.
items.markingKey: order 3 > 4 > 1 > 2 [2]; explanation referring to each factor varied [2]

items.stem: Sofia plans an investigation into how the rate of reaction between magnesium and hydrochloric acid can be changed. (a) Name the independent variable and two control variables for an investigation into the effect of temperature. (b) Explain why the experiment should be repeated. (c) Suggest one safety precaution.
items.answer: (a) independent: temperature; control: concentration and volume of acid, mass and size of magnesium (b) to identify anomalous results and calculate a reliable mean (c) wear eye protection (acid); no naked flames near hydrogen
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark independent; 1 mark controls [2] (b) [1] (c) [1]

items.stem: Amara plans an investigation into how the rate of reaction between iron and hydrochloric acid can be changed. (a) State three changes that would increase the rate of reaction. (b) Explain why increasing the temperature by 10 °C can roughly double the rate.
items.answer: (a) increase acid concentration; increase temperature; use smaller pieces / powder (or add a catalyst) (b) particles move faster, collide more often and a much larger proportion have energy ≥ Ea
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [3] (b) [2]

items.stem: What is a catalyst?
options: a substance that increases the rate of a reaction and is unchanged chemically at the end
a reactant that is used up
a substance that slows a reaction down
items.answer: a substance that increases the rate of a reaction and is unchanged chemically at the end
items.markingKey: Catalysts speed up reactions without being used up.

items.stem: Explain why the total volume of gas produced is the same when the same mass of magnesium reacts with excess acid at two different temperatures.
items.answer: The amount of product depends on the amount of limiting reactant (magnesium), which is the same; temperature only changes how fast the gas is made.

items.stem: Describe a fair test to investigate the effect of acid concentration on the rate of reaction with magnesium.
items.answer: Change only the concentration; keep the volume of acid, mass/length of magnesium, temperature and surface area the same; measure the volume of gas over time or the time for the reaction to finish.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: one independent variable; 1 mark: two controls; 1 mark: measurement [3]

items.stem: Daniel doubles the concentration of the hydrochloric acid in the reaction between calcium carbonate (marble) small chips and hydrochloric acid, keeping all other variables the same. Predict the effect on the rate and on the total volume of carbon dioxide produced if the solid is the limiting reactant.
items.answer: The rate increases; the total volume of carbon dioxide stays the same because the amount of limiting reactant is unchanged.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: rate increases; 1 mark: reason (factor); 1 mark: same final volume, same amount of limiting reactant [3]

items.stem: Hana varies the conditions for the reaction of magnesium with hydrochloric acid, keeping the mass of solid and volume of acid the same. experiment 1: ribbon, 1.00 mol/dm³ acid, 40 °C; experiment 2: ribbon, 1.00 mol/dm³ acid, 25 °C; experiment 3: ribbon, 1.00 mol/dm³ acid, 60 °C. Which experiment has the fastest initial rate?
items.answer: experiment 3
items.markingKey: Experiment 3 has conditions at least as favourable in every factor (concentration, temperature, surface area) and better in at least one.

items.stem: Grace varies the conditions for the reaction of iron with hydrochloric acid, keeping the mass of solid and volume of acid the same. experiment 1: filings, 1.00 mol/dm³ acid, 35 °C; experiment 2: nails, 1.00 mol/dm³ acid, 25 °C; experiment 3: filings, 1.00 mol/dm³ acid, 25 °C. Which experiment has the fastest initial rate?
items.answer: experiment 1
items.markingKey: Experiment 1 has conditions at least as favourable in every factor (concentration, temperature, surface area) and better in at least one.

items.stem: Nadia varies the conditions for the reaction of zinc with sulfuric acid, keeping the mass of solid and volume of acid the same. experiment 1: large granules, 0.500 mol/dm³ acid, 15 °C; experiment 2: small granules, 0.500 mol/dm³ acid, 15 °C; experiment 3: small granules, 2.00 mol/dm³ acid, 15 °C. Which experiment has the fastest initial rate?
items.answer: experiment 3
items.markingKey: Experiment 3 has conditions at least as favourable in every factor (concentration, temperature, surface area) and better in at least one.

items.stem: Nadia, a student in Bogotá, reacts zinc with sulfuric acid, using the same mass of solid and volume of acid each time. experiment 1: small granules, 0.500 mol/dm³ acid, 60 °C; experiment 2: small granules, 0.500 mol/dm³ acid, 30 °C; experiment 3: small granules, 0.500 mol/dm³ acid, 15 °C; experiment 4: small granules, 0.500 mol/dm³ acid, 50 °C. Put the experiments in order of initial rate, fastest first, and explain your order.
items.answer: Order: 1 > 4 > 2 > 3. Higher concentration, higher temperature and smaller pieces (larger surface area) each increase the rate.
items.markingKey: order 1 > 4 > 2 > 3 [2]; explanation referring to each factor varied [2]

items.stem: Samuel, a student in Dhaka, reacts calcium carbonate with hydrochloric acid, using the same mass of solid and volume of acid each time. experiment 1: large lumps, 1.00 mol/dm³ acid, 60 °C; experiment 2: large lumps, 1.00 mol/dm³ acid, 45 °C; experiment 3: large lumps, 0.500 mol/dm³ acid, 25 °C; experiment 4: large lumps, 1.00 mol/dm³ acid, 25 °C. Put the experiments in order of initial rate, fastest first, and explain your order.
items.answer: Order: 1 > 2 > 4 > 3. Higher concentration, higher temperature and smaller pieces (larger surface area) each increase the rate.
items.markingKey: order 1 > 2 > 4 > 3 [2]; explanation referring to each factor varied [2]

items.stem: A company in Seoul wants to make carbon dioxide faster from calcium carbonate and hydrochloric acid. (a) Name the independent variable and two control variables for an investigation into the effect of temperature. (b) Explain why the experiment should be repeated. (c) Suggest one safety precaution.
items.answer: (a) independent: temperature; control: concentration and volume of acid, mass and size of calcium carbonate (b) to identify anomalous results and calculate a reliable mean (c) wear eye protection; avoid acid on skin
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark independent; 1 mark controls [2] (b) [1] (c) [1]

items.stem: A company in Colombo wants to make hydrogen faster from zinc and sulfuric acid. (a) Describe how the rate could be measured. (b) Name the independent variable and two control variables for an investigation into the effect of temperature.
items.answer: (a) measure the volume of hydrogen produced at regular time intervals with a gas syringe (or mass loss on a balance) (b) independent: temperature; control: concentration and volume of acid, mass and size of zinc
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark apparatus; 1 mark timed readings [2] (b) 1 mark independent; 1 mark controls [2]

items.stem: According to collision theory, what must happen for particles to react?
options: They must collide with a catalyst.
They must be in the same state.
They must collide with at least the activation energy.
items.answer: They must collide with at least the activation energy.
items.markingKey: Successful collisions need energy ≥ Ea.

items.stem: Explain, using collision theory, why powdered calcium carbonate reacts faster with acid than lumps of the same mass.
items.answer: The powder has a larger surface area, so more particles are exposed to the acid; collisions are more frequent.

items.stem: Explain why a small increase in temperature can cause a large increase in rate.
items.answer: A higher temperature increases the energy of the particles, so a much greater proportion of collisions have energy ≥ Ea, as well as increasing collision frequency.

items.stem: Arjun measures the time for magnesium to react with acid at different temperatures: 20 °C: 210 s, 30 °C: 95 s, 40 °C: 50 s, 50 °C: 25 s. Describe the trend and explain it using collision theory.
items.answer: As temperature increases the time decreases, so the rate increases (roughly doubling every 10 °C): particles move faster, collide more often, and more collisions have energy ≥ Ea.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: faster at higher temperature; 1 mark: more frequent and more energetic collisions [2]

items.stem: Kwame measures the time taken for a fixed amount of magnesium ribbon to react completely with excess hydrochloric acid at different temperatures: 30 °C: 150 s, 40 °C: 75 s, 50 °C: 36 s, 60 °C: 18 s. Describe the effect of temperature on the time and on the rate, calculate the rate (1/time) at 30 °C and 60 °C, and explain the trend using collision theory.
items.answer: As temperature increases the time decreases and the rate increases (roughly doubling every 10 °C). Rate at 30 °C = 6.67 × 10⁻³ /s; at 60 °C = 5.56 × 10⁻² /s. Particles move faster, collide more often, and more collisions have energy ≥ Ea.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: time decreases / rate increases; 1 mark: rates calculated; 1 mark: more frequent collisions; 1 mark: more collisions with energy ≥ Ea [4]

items.stem: A cleaning-products company in Bangkok studies how fast hydrogen peroxide decomposes to oxygen and water. (a) Explain why the reaction is faster at a higher temperature. (b) Suggest why the company stores hydrogen peroxide in a cool, dark place.
items.answer: (a) particles faster: more frequent collisions; greater proportion with energy ≥ Ea (b) lower temperature (and no light energy) slows the decomposition

items.stem: Why does increasing the concentration of an acid increase the rate of reaction?
options: There are more particles per unit volume, so there are more frequent collisions.
items.answer: There are more particles per unit volume, so there are more frequent collisions.
items.markingKey: Collision frequency increases.

items.stem: Explain why the rate of reaction decreases as a reaction proceeds.
items.answer: The reactants are used up, so their concentration decreases and collisions become less frequent.

items.stem: Explain why increasing the pressure has no effect on the rate of a reaction between a solid and a liquid.
items.answer: Pressure only affects gases; it changes how close together gas particles are, but has no significant effect on liquids and solids.

items.stem: Noah measures the time for magnesium to react with acid at different temperatures: 30 °C: 142 s, 40 °C: 75 s, 50 °C: 38 s, 60 °C: 20 s. Describe the trend and explain it using collision theory.
items.answer: As temperature increases the time decreases, so the rate increases (roughly doubling every 10 °C): particles move faster, collide more often, and more collisions have energy ≥ Ea.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: faster at higher temperature; 1 mark: more frequent and more energetic collisions [2]

items.stem: Zara measures the time for magnesium to react with acid at different temperatures: 30 °C: 240 s, 40 °C: 126 s, 50 °C: 60 s, 60 °C: 30 s. Describe the trend and explain it using collision theory.
items.answer: As temperature increases the time decreases, so the rate increases (roughly doubling every 10 °C): particles move faster, collide more often, and more collisions have energy ≥ Ea.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: faster at higher temperature; 1 mark: more frequent and more energetic collisions [2]

items.stem: Elena measures the time taken for a fixed amount of magnesium ribbon to react completely with excess hydrochloric acid at different temperatures: 25 °C: 189 s, 35 °C: 90 s, 45 °C: 43 s, 55 °C: 22 s. Describe the effect of temperature on the time and on the rate, calculate the rate (1/time) at 25 °C and 55 °C, and explain the trend using collision theory.
items.answer: As temperature increases the time decreases and the rate increases (roughly doubling every 10 °C). Rate at 25 °C = 5.29 × 10⁻³ /s; at 55 °C = 4.55 × 10⁻² /s. Particles move faster, collide more often, and more collisions have energy ≥ Ea.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: time decreases / rate increases; 1 mark: rates calculated; 1 mark: more frequent collisions; 1 mark: more collisions with energy ≥ Ea [4]

items.stem: Noah compares the rate of decomposition of hydrogen peroxide, 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂, with and without manganese(IV) oxide, and at two different temperatures. (a) Describe how you could show that the manganese(IV) oxide is not used up. (b) Explain why the rate decreases as the reaction proceeds. (c) Suggest why the company stores hydrogen peroxide in a cool, dark place.
items.answer: (a) filter, wash and dry the catalyst after the reaction and weigh it – same mass; it can catalyse again (b) concentration of H₂O₂ falls, so fewer collisions per second (c) lower temperature (and no light energy) slows the decomposition

items.stem: Which apparatus is used to measure the volume of gas produced in a reaction?
items.answer: gas syringe
items.markingKey: A gas syringe collects and measures gas volume.

items.stem: Explain why the gradient of a volume–time graph is steepest at the start of a reaction.
items.answer: The concentration of reactants is highest at the start, so collisions are most frequent and the rate is greatest.

items.stem: Explain why measuring the loss in mass is not a good method for a reaction that produces hydrogen.
items.answer: Hydrogen has a very low mass (Mr = 2), so the change in mass is too small to measure accurately.

items.stem: Mei adds 0.130 g of zinc powder to excess sulfuric acid and collects the H₂ in a gas syringe. Results: 0 s: 0 cm³, 15 s: 27 cm³, 30 s: 39 cm³, 45 s: 44 cm³, 60 s: 46 cm³, 75 s: 47 cm³, 90 s: 48 cm³, 105 s: 48 cm³. Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂ Describe how the rate changes during the reaction and explain why.
items.answer: fastest at the start, decreases, then zero when reaction stops; reactant concentration decreases / limiting reactant used up
items.markingKey: 1 mark description; 1 mark explanation [2]

items.stem: Ines adds 0.130 g of zinc powder to excess sulfuric acid and collects the H₂ in a gas syringe. Results: 0 s: 0 cm³, 15 s: 23 cm³, 30 s: 35 cm³, 45 s: 42 cm³, 60 s: 45 cm³, 75 s: 46 cm³, 90 s: 48 cm³, 105 s: 48 cm³. Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂ (a) Describe how the results would differ if the experiment were repeated at a higher temperature with the same mass of zinc powder. (b) Calculate the rate between 15 s and 30 s.
items.answer: (a) steeper initial gradient (faster); same final volume, reached sooner (b) 0.800 cm³/s

items.stem: Sipho reacts 0.120 g of magnesium ribbon with 50 cm³ of 1.0 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid (excess) at 25 °C. Volume of H₂: 0 s: 0 cm³, 20 s: 53 cm³, 40 s: 83 cm³, 60 s: 99 cm³, 80 s: 108 cm³, 100 s: 114 cm³, 120 s: 120 cm³, 140 s: 120 cm³. (Ar: Mg = 24) (a) Calculate the theoretical final volume of gas at r.t.p. (b) Evaluate whether a gas syringe or mass-loss method is better for this reaction.
items.answer: (a) 120 cm³ (b) gas syringe: hydrogen too light for mass loss

items.stem: Describe how the graph would differ if the same reaction were repeated with half the mass of the limiting reactant at the same temperature.
items.answer: The initial gradient would be similar or slightly less, and the final volume would be half as much.

items.stem: Explain why "1/time" can be used as a measure of the rate in the disappearing-cross experiment.
items.answer: The same amount of sulfur is formed each time; a shorter time means a faster rate, so rate is proportional to 1/time.

items.stem: Describe how the rate of reaction between zinc powder and sulfuric acid could be followed using a upturned measuring cylinder method, and state what is plotted on the graph.
items.answer: Collect the gas over water in an upturned measuring cylinder; record the volume at regular intervals; plot volume of gas against time.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: apparatus; 1 mark: readings at regular time intervals; 1 mark: graph axes [3]

items.stem: 80 cm³ of H₂ is produced in the first 50 s when zinc powder reacts with sulfuric acid. Calculate the average rate in cm³/s and in cm³/min.
items.answer: 1.60 cm³/s; 96.0 cm³/min

items.stem: 56 cm³ of H₂ is produced in the first 120 s when magnesium ribbon reacts with hydrochloric acid. Calculate the average rate in cm³/s and in cm³/min.
items.answer: 0.467 cm³/s; 28.0 cm³/min

items.stem: Ines reacts 0.120 g of magnesium ribbon with 50 cm³ of 1.0 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid (excess) at 25 °C. Volume of H₂: 0 s: 0 cm³, 20 s: 68 cm³, 40 s: 97 cm³, 60 s: 110 cm³, 80 s: 116 cm³, 100 s: 118 cm³, 120 s: 120 cm³, 140 s: 120 cm³. (Ar: Mg = 24) (a) Describe the curve if half the mass of solid were used with the original acid. (b) Evaluate whether a gas syringe or mass-loss method is better for this reaction.
items.answer: (a) slightly less steep at first; final volume halved (≈ 60.0 cm³) (b) gas syringe: hydrogen too light for mass loss

items.stem: Lucas reacts 0.120 g of magnesium ribbon with 50 cm³ of 1.0 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid (excess) at 25 °C. Volume of H₂: 0 s: 0 cm³, 20 s: 68 cm³, 40 s: 97 cm³, 60 s: 110 cm³, 80 s: 116 cm³, 100 s: 118 cm³, 120 s: 120 cm³, 140 s: 120 cm³. (Ar: Mg = 24) (a) Calculate the theoretical final volume of gas at r.t.p. (b) Describe the curve you would expect if 25 cm³ of 2.0 mol/dm³ acid were used instead, with the same solid. (c) Evaluate whether a gas syringe or mass-loss method is better for this reaction.
items.answer: (a) 120 cm³ (b) steeper at the start (more concentrated); same final volume (same amount of limiting solid) (c) gas syringe: hydrogen too light for mass loss

items.stem: Which observation is a sign of a chemical change?
options: Bubbles of gas form when two solutions are mixed.
Sugar disappears when stirred into water.
items.answer: Bubbles of gas form when two solutions are mixed.
items.markingKey: Gas evolution from a reaction indicates a new substance.

items.stem: Explain why the total mass stays the same in both physical and chemical changes in a closed container.
items.answer: Atoms are not created or destroyed; they are only rearranged (chemical) or move apart/closer (physical).

items.stem: Classify each change as physical or chemical: ink being separated by chromatography; iodine subliming when warmed; silver tarnishing; copper(II) carbonate turning black when heated.
items.answer: ink being separated by chromatography: physical; iodine subliming when warmed: physical; silver tarnishing: chemical; copper(II) carbonate turning black when heated: chemical
items.markingKey: ink being separated by chromatography: physical; iodine subliming when warmed: physical; silver tarnishing: chemical; copper(II) carbonate turning black when heated: chemical. 1 mark per two correct [2]

(b) Write the symbol equation for the decomposition. (c) Explain why melting the wax is a physical change. (d) Explain why the mass of the test tube and contents decreases.

items.stem: Which catalyst is used to speed up the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide?
items.answer: manganese(IV) oxide
items.markingKey: MnO₂ catalyses 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂.

items.stem: Diego uses powdered magnesium instead of ribbon in the reaction between magnesium turnings and hydrochloric acid, keeping all other variables the same. Predict the effect on the rate and on the total volume of hydrogen produced if the solid is the limiting reactant.
items.answer: The rate increases; the total volume of hydrogen stays the same because the amount of limiting reactant is unchanged.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: rate increases; 1 mark: same total volume with reason [2]

items.markingKey: Experiment 3 has conditions at least as favourable in every factor (concentration, temperature, surface area) and better in at least one.

items.stem: In an IGCSE practical lesson, the rate of reaction of zinc with sulfuric acid is compared. experiment 1: powder, 0.500 mol/dm³ acid, 15 °C; experiment 2: large granules, 0.500 mol/dm³ acid, 15 °C; experiment 3: small granules, 0.500 mol/dm³ acid, 15 °C. Which experiment has the fastest initial rate?
items.answer: experiment 1
items.markingKey: Experiment 1 has conditions at least as favourable in every factor (concentration, temperature, surface area) and better in at least one.

items.stem: A company in Riyadh wants to make hydrogen faster from magnesium and hydrochloric acid. (a) Name the independent variable and two control variables for an investigation into the effect of temperature. (b) Explain why the experiment should be repeated. (c) Suggest one safety precaution.
items.answer: (a) independent: temperature; control: concentration and volume of acid, mass and size of magnesium (b) to identify anomalous results and calculate a reliable mean (c) wear eye protection (acid); no naked flames near hydrogen
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark independent; 1 mark controls [2] (b) [1] (c) [1]

items.stem: Which statement explains why the rate increases when a catalyst is added?
options: Particles have more kinetic energy and move faster, so they collide more frequently and a greater proportion of collisions have energy greater than or equal to the activation energy.
There are more reacting particles per unit volume, so collisions are more frequent (more collisions per second).
It provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, so a greater proportion of collisions are successful.
items.answer: It provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, so a greater proportion of collisions are successful.
items.markingKey: It provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, so a greater proportion of collisions are successful.

items.stem: In the reaction between iron and hydrochloric acid, the iron is used as a powder instead of nails. Explain, using collision theory, why the rate increases.
items.answer: More particles of the solid are exposed to the other reactant, so collisions are more frequent.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: more particles per unit volume / closer / exposed; 1 mark: more frequent collisions (per second) [2]

items.stem: Kenji measures the time for magnesium to react with acid at different temperatures: 20 °C: 171 s, 30 °C: 90 s, 40 °C: 43 s, 50 °C: 24 s. Describe the trend and explain it using collision theory.
items.answer: As temperature increases the time decreases, so the rate increases (roughly doubling every 10 °C): particles move faster, collide more often, and more collisions have energy ≥ Ea.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: faster at higher temperature; 1 mark: more frequent and more energetic collisions [2]

Describe the effect of temperature on the time and on the rate, calculate the rate (1/time) at 30 °C and 60 °C, and explain the trend using collision theory.
items.answer: As temperature increases the time decreases and the rate increases (roughly doubling every 10 °C). Rate at 30 °C = 5.56 × 10⁻³ /s; at 60 °C = 4.55 × 10⁻² /s. Particles move faster, collide more often, and more collisions have energy ≥ Ea.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: time decreases / rate increases; 1 mark: rates calculated; 1 mark: more frequent collisions; 1 mark: more collisions with energy ≥ Ea [4]

items.stem: Felix compares the rate of decomposition of hydrogen peroxide, 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂, with and without manganese(IV) oxide, and at two different temperatures. (a) Explain what is meant by activation energy. (b) Describe how you could show that the manganese(IV) oxide is not used up. (c) Suggest why the company stores hydrogen peroxide in a cool, dark place.
items.answer: (a) minimum energy colliding particles need to react (b) filter, wash and dry the catalyst after the reaction and weigh it – same mass; it can catalyse again (c) lower temperature (and no light energy) slows the decomposition

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why "1/time" can be used as a measure of the rate in the disappearing-cross experiment. (b) Explain why measuring the loss in mass is not a good method for a reaction that produces hydrogen.
items.answer: (a) The same amount of sulfur is formed each time; a shorter time means a faster rate, so rate is proportional to 1/time. (b) Hydrogen has a very low mass (Mr = 2), so the change in mass is too small to measure accurately.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why "1/time" can be used as a measure of the rate in the disappearing-cross experiment. (b) Explain why the gradient of a volume–time graph is steepest at the start of a reaction.
items.answer: (a) The same amount of sulfur is formed each time; a shorter time means a faster rate, so rate is proportional to 1/time. (b) The concentration of reactants is highest at the start, so collisions are most frequent and the rate is greatest.

items.stem: Priya times how long it takes for a cross under a flask to disappear when hydrochloric acid is added to sodium thiosulfate solution of different concentrations: 0.0400 mol/dm³: 120 s, 0.0800 mol/dm³: 60 s, 0.120 mol/dm³: 40 s, 0.160 mol/dm³: 30 s, 0.200 mol/dm³: 24 s. Calculate 1000/time for the most and least concentrated solutions, describe the relationship between concentration and rate, and explain why the cross disappears.
items.answer: 1000/t = 41.7 and 8.33 /s; rate is (directly) proportional to concentration – doubling the concentration halves the time. A precipitate of sulfur forms and hides the cross.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: both values of 1000/t; 1 mark: rate increases with concentration; 1 mark: proportional/doubling halves time; 1 mark: sulfur precipitate [4]

items.stem: State one difference between a physical change and a chemical change.
items.answer: In a chemical change a new substance is formed; in a physical change no new substance forms.

items.stem: Isla observes iron rusting. State whether this is a physical or a chemical change and explain your answer.
items.answer: Chemical: a new substance is formed; the change is usually difficult to reverse.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: classification; 1 mark: reason [2]

items.stem: Classify each change as physical or chemical: salt being separated from sea water by evaporation; water being electrolysed; wax melting; wood burning.
items.answer: salt being separated from sea water by evaporation: physical; water being electrolysed: chemical; wax melting: physical; wood burning: chemical
items.markingKey: salt being separated from sea water by evaporation: physical; water being electrolysed: chemical; wax melting: physical; wood burning: chemical. 1 mark per two correct [2]

items.stem: Sofia heats 6.18 g of white zinc carbonate, ZnCO₃, in a test tube. The solid turns yellow when hot, white when cool and a gas is given off that turns limewater milky. A separate sample of wax is heated: it melts and then solidifies again on cooling. (a) State whether each change is physical or chemical. (b) Calculate the mass of solid left after complete decomposition. (Ar: C = 12, O = 16, Zn = 65) (c) Explain why melting the wax is a physical change. (d) Explain why the mass of the test tube and contents decreases.
items.answer: (a) heating zinc carbonate: chemical; melting wax: physical (b) 4.00 g (c) no new substance; the wax solidifies again unchanged (d) carbon dioxide gas escapes

items.stem: For a reaction between gases, which change increases the rate?
options: increasing the volume of the container
items.answer: increasing the pressure
items.markingKey: Particles closer together → more frequent collisions.

items.stem: Noah adds a few drops of copper(II) sulfate solution as a catalyst in the reaction between zinc small granules and sulfuric acid, keeping all other variables the same. Predict the effect on the rate and on the total volume of hydrogen produced if the solid is the limiting reactant.
items.answer: The rate increases; the total volume of hydrogen stays the same because the amount of limiting reactant is unchanged.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: rate increases; 1 mark: same total volume with reason [2]

items.stem: Ines warms the sulfuric acid from 20 °C to 40 °C in the reaction between zinc small granules and sulfuric acid, keeping all other variables the same. Predict the effect on the rate and on the total volume of hydrogen produced if the solid is the limiting reactant.

items.stem: In a teaching laboratory, the rate of reaction of calcium carbonate with hydrochloric acid is compared. experiment 1: small chips, 0.250 mol/dm³ acid, 25 °C; experiment 2: powder, 0.250 mol/dm³ acid, 45 °C; experiment 3: small chips, 0.250 mol/dm³ acid, 45 °C. items.answer: experiment 2

items.answer: experiment 2

items.stem: Priya plans an investigation into how the rate of reaction between calcium carbonate and hydrochloric acid can be changed. (a) State three changes that would increase the rate of reaction. (b) Suggest one safety precaution.

items.stem: Which statement explains why the rate increases when a solid reactant is crushed into a powder?
options: More particles of the solid are exposed to the other reactant, so collisions are more frequent.
The gas particles are closer together, so collisions are more frequent.
It provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, so a greater proportion of collisions are successful.
items.answer: More particles of the solid are exposed to the other reactant, so collisions are more frequent.
items.markingKey: More particles of the solid are exposed to the other reactant, so collisions are more frequent.

items.stem: Hana writes: "Increasing the temperature increases the activation energy." Explain why this statement is incorrect and give a correct statement.
items.answer: Activation energy is unchanged by temperature; more particles have energy ≥ Ea.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: error identified; 1 mark: correct statement [2]

items.stem: Felix measures the time for magnesium to react with acid at different temperatures: 20 °C: 120 s, 30 °C: 57 s, 40 °C: 28 s, 50 °C: 16 s. Describe the trend and explain it using collision theory.
